chapters.title: 8. Saddleback Church and the Montgomery Bus Boycott: How Movements Happen

assets.domain: Habit Loops | Behavioral Friction & Choice Architecture
assets.topic: The three-part social-habit formula of movements
assets.visual_frame_description: A classroom-style sorting board fills the screen. Three labeled columns stand side by side, and a stack of evidence cards about Rosa Parks's arrest and Rick Warren's church sits beside them. As the player drags each card into a column, the card snaps into place and reveals whether the label is a strong-tie friendship habit, a weak-tie community pressure, or a new habit that builds identity. The setting shifts between a 1955 Montgomery print shop and a modern Orange County living room.
assets.player_mission: Sort each evidence card into exactly one of the three columns of the movement formula from the book. Read the evidence carefully and decide which of the three mechanisms is driving the behavior described, then confirm your classification of the focal card about the newspaper headline.
key_concepts: A movement starts because of the social habits of friendship and the strong ties between close acquaintances.
A movement grows because of the habits of a community and the weak ties that hold neighborhoods and clans together.
A movement endures because leaders give participants new habits that create a fresh sense of identity and a feeling of ownership.
Usually only when all three parts of the process are fulfilled can a movement become self-propelling and reach a critical mass.
Social habits are behaviors that occur unthinkingly across dozens, hundreds, or thousands of people and can fill streets with protesters.
Rosa Parks was arrested on December 1, 1955, and her friends across dozens of Montgomery networks responded within hours.
The Advertiser ran an article implying that every black citizen would join the boycott, which made residents assume everyone else was already on board.
Jo Ann Robinson distributed mimeographed flyers through schoolteachers to parents and coworkers within twenty-four hours.
Rick Warren assigned every Saddleback member to a weekly small group so participation became a habit drawing on existing social urges.
Saddleback members sign a maturity covenant card promising daily quiet time, tithing 10 percent of income, and small-group membership.
assets.theory_summary: This matrix tests the three-part mechanism behind social movements: movements ignite through strong-tie friendship habits, spread through weak-tie community expectations, and endure when leaders install new habits that reshape identity. Duhigg presents this as the recurring recipe that turned Rosa Parks's arrest into the Montgomery bus boycott and scaled Rick Warren's Saddleback Church.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits)

assets.question: Which column does the Advertiser's 'every black citizen is expected to join Monday's boycott' headline belong to, given that only Parks's friends, the ministers, and the organizers had actually committed at the time?
assets.column_b_label: Weak ties (community expectations and peer pressure)
assets.column_c_label: New habits that build self-identity and ownership

rows.label: E. D. Nixon phones King's closest friend, Ralph Abernathy, to help persuade the hesitant young minister to join the boycott.
The Advertiser publishes that 'every black citizen' will join Monday's boycott, so residents assume everyone else is already on board.
Saddleback asks every member to sign a maturity covenant card promising daily quiet time, tithing, and small-group membership.
Jo Ann Robinson's teachers distribute mimeographed flyers through parents and coworkers across the city.
After the bombing of his house, King gives crowds the habit of answering violence with nonviolence and forgiveness.
Parks's friends in the NAACP, churches, and volunteer circles post bail and agree to show their support.

distractors: Column a, because newspapers are passed around within tight friendship circles.
Column c, because reading a headline permanently changes a person's self-concept.
Column a, because the headline only mattered to the organizers who printed the flyers.
assets.explanation: The headline sorts to column b: when residents read that 'every black citizen' would participate, they assumed the community was already committed and feared that being seen on a bus Monday would look bad. That is exactly the authority of communal expectations and peer pressure that spreads through weak ties, which Duhigg describes as the second part of the movement formula.

assets.domain: Habit Loops | Behavioral Friction & Choice Architecture
assets.topic: Weak ties and the flow of job information
assets.visual_frame_description: A university office in the late 1960s is shown, with a bulletin board covered in strings connecting labeled name cards. In the center, a researcher's notepad tallies how 282 men found their jobs. Some name cards are clustered in dense cliques, while long thin strings link distant clusters. The player studies the web to identify which kinds of connections carried job leads.
assets.player_mission: Examine each connection on the network board and classify whether it is a strong tie, a weak tie, or an isolated redundant link. Then answer why casual acquaintances, rather than close friends, so often delivered job leads in Granovetter's study.
key_concepts: In the late 1960s, Harvard PhD student Mark Granovetter studied how 282 men had found their current employment.
Granovetter called connections to casual acquaintances 'weak ties' because they link people who share membership in networks but are not directly bound by friendship.
Job hunters were often rejected by strangers and helped by close friends, but help also came surprisingly often from casual acquaintances.
Weak ties give access to social networks where a person does not otherwise belong.
Close friends tend to know the same information a person already knows, so they rarely deliver genuinely new opportunities.
Granovetter wrote that individuals with few weak ties are deprived of information from distant parts of the social system.
Without weak ties, momentum generated inside a clique does not spread beyond the clique.
Duhigg argues the power of weak ties explains how a protest can expand from a group of friends into a broad social movement.
Peer pressure spreads through weak ties and gains its authority through communal expectations.
Weak-tie acquaintances are often as influential as, or more influential than, close-tie friends when opinions move through communities.
assets.theory_summary: This matrix tests Granovetter's weak-ties finding: casual acquaintances connect us to networks we do not otherwise belong to, while close friends tend to share the same information we already have. Duhigg uses the finding to explain why communities and political movements spread through weak ties rather than through tight friendship cliques.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits)

assets.question: Which column best captures why Granovetter's job hunters so often learned about openings from casual acquaintances rather than from their closest friends?
assets.column_c_label: Isolation (few or no ties to other networks)

rows.label: A job hunter hears about an opening from a former colleague she sees only twice a year.
Close friends learn about a new opening, but everyone in the tight group already knows about it.
An applicant with few weak ties learns only what his immediate circle already knows and hears nothing from distant parts of the social system.
A friend of a friend passes along a referral to a network the job hunter does not otherwise belong to.
Two siblings who talk every day share the same internship lead within hours of each other.
A protest organizer only canvasses the members of one tight clique, and the momentum never spreads to the rest of the city.

distractors: Column a, because only the people you trust most would risk recommending you to an employer.
Column c, because casual acquaintances are too far from the job hunter to matter at all.
Column a, because all job leads ultimately travel through first-hand friendships.
assets.explanation: The focal case sorts to column b: a former colleague seen twice a year is a classic weak tie, and weak ties delivered many of the job leads in Granovetter's study because they reach networks where the job hunter does not otherwise belong. Close friends (column a) tend to know the same things the job hunter already knows, and isolation (column c) is what deprives people of distant information.

assets.domain: Habit Loops | Behavioral Friction & Choice Architecture
assets.topic: Why Parks ignited the boycott when earlier arrests did not
assets.visual_frame_description: A Montgomery jailhouse hallway in 1955 is depicted, with a wall of arrest photographs: Geneva Johnson, Viola White, Katie Wingfield, Claudette Colvin, Mary Louise Smith, and Rosa Parks. Icons below each photo show how many protesters it sparked. Parks's photo glows and links outward to a web of churches, clubs, and volunteer groups, while the others stand alone in the frame.
assets.player_mission: Classify each piece of evidence as community embeddedness, legal and political climate, or individual act alone. Then decide which factor best explains why Parks's arrest, and not the earlier arrests, ignited the boycott.
key_concepts: Parks was the secretary of the local NAACP chapter, attended the Methodist church, and helped oversee a youth organization at a Lutheran church.
Parks volunteered at a shelter, joined a botanical club, and knit blankets with a women's group on Wednesday nights.
Parks's friendships spanned the city's hierarchies, from field hands to college professors.
Geneva Johnson, Viola White, Katie Wingfield, Claudette Colvin, and Mary Louise Smith were all arrested for bus seating and none of those arrests produced a boycott.
Montgomery residents treated Brown v. Board as an abstraction from a far-off courthouse.
Brown v. Board and Brown II still created a powerful national sense that change was in the air.
E. D. Nixon and lawyer Clifford Durr bailed Parks out and had been looking for the perfect case to challenge the bus law.
Parks's many memberships allowed her friends to muster a response before the community's normal apathy could take hold.
Studies show people have no problem ignoring strangers' injuries, but when a friend is insulted the sense of outrage can overcome the inertia that makes protests hard to organize.
Taylor Branch wrote that Parks was one of those rare people of whom everyone agreed that she gave more than she got.
assets.theory_summary: This matrix tests why strong-tie friendship habits, rather than legal precedent or individual defiance alone, turned Parks's arrest into the first mass movement of the modern civil rights era. Duhigg argues that Parks's deep community embeddedness let her friends react before the community's normal apathy took hold, something the earlier arrests of equally defiant riders could not trigger.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits)

assets.question: Which column best explains why Rosa Parks's arrest ignited the boycott when the earlier arrests of Claudette Colvin and Mary Louise Smith did not?

rows.label: Parks was secretary of the local NAACP and belonged to dozens of groups spanning the city's racial and economic lines.
Colvin and Mary Louise Smith were arrested after Brown v. Board yet sparked no protest.
Brown v. Board and Brown II gave Montgomery residents a sense that change was in the air.
Nixon and Durr had been waiting for the perfect test case and bailed Parks out within hours of her arrest.
Parks's friends could muster a response before the community's normal apathy could take hold.
A single act of defiance on a crowded bus, by itself, rarely produces a boycott.

distractors: Column b, because only the Supreme Court's rulings could ever produce a mass protest.
Column c, because Parks was simply braver than the other riders who were arrested.
Column b, because Parks's arrest happened months after Brown II, unlike the earlier arrests.
assets.explanation: The focal case sorts to column a: Parks's deep, cross-cutting network of friendships meant her arrest activated the social habits of friendship immediately, and her allies could rally before apathy set in. Column b is insufficient because Colvin and Mary Louise Smith were arrested after Brown v. Board yet sparked nothing, and column c fails because countless defiant riders before Parks were jailed without a boycott.

assets.domain: Habit Loops | Behavioral Friction & Choice Architecture
assets.visual_frame_description: A 1980s Arizona university archive desk holds a stack of yellowed five-page Freedom Summer applications from 1964. A sociologist's charts plot motivations, job status, marriage status, and web diagrams of each applicant's club memberships. Three hypothesis labels hang over the desk as the player sorts which explanation the data actually supported.
assets.player_mission: Classify each finding by which of McAdam's hypotheses it belongs to or refutes. Then determine what the 720 applications revealed about why some accepted students boarded the bus for Mississippi while more than three hundred stayed home.
key_concepts: In the 1980s, sociologist Doug McAdam at the University of Arizona read 720 five-page Freedom Summer applications from 1964.
McAdam's initial hypothesis was that students who went to Mississippi had different motivations from those who stayed home.
The selfish and the selfless went South in equal numbers; differences in motives explained no significant distinctions between participants and withdrawals.
Being married or holding a full-time job actually enhanced the applicant's chances of going south.
Applicants were asked to list their memberships and at least ten people they wanted kept informed of their summer activities.
Students who participated were enmeshed in communities where both their close friends and their casual acquaintances expected them to get on the bus.
Applicants in newspaper, student government, academic, and fraternity groups could withdraw with little or no loss of social standing.
Among applicants with a religious orientation who belonged to a religious organization, every single one made the trip to Mississippi.
Once a community knew a student had been accepted into Freedom Summer, withdrawing threatened a large amount of social standing.
Applying for Freedom Summer was not a casual undertaking, with essays, references, and interviews.
assets.theory_summary: This matrix tests McAdam's finding that social networks, not motives or opportunity costs, predicted who participated in Freedom Summer: students embedded in communities where strong and weak ties expected them to go boarded the bus, while equally motivated students in permissive communities stayed home. Duhigg presents this as evidence that social habits, rather than individual conviction, drive who joins a movement.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits)

assets.question: Which factor actually predicted whether an accepted applicant went to Mississippi in the Mississippi Summer Project?

rows.label: Applicants who wanted to 'test myself' went South in equal numbers to those who wanted to 'improve the lot of blacks.'
Being married or holding a full-time job enhanced the applicant's chances of going south.
Applicants whose close friends also applied for Freedom Summer were far more likely to buy a bus ticket.
Every applicant with a religious orientation who belonged to a religious organization made the trip.
Students in newspaper, student government, and fraternity groups could withdraw with little loss of standing.
McAdam's initial hypothesis that different motivations explained the divergence turned out to be wrong.

distractors: Column a, because the other-oriented students were the only ones willing to risk their lives for the cause.
Column b, because applicants with jobs and families rationally chose safety over activism.
Column b, because married students were less free to travel and therefore withdrew more often.
assets.explanation: The focal case sorts to column c: McAdam's network analysis of memberships and contact lists revealed that participants were enmeshed in communities where both strong and weak ties expected them to go. Columns a and b were explicitly refuted by the data, since motives were equally distributed and married or employed applicants were actually more likely to go.

assets.topic: Saddleback's reverse structure and self-feeding members
assets.visual_frame_description: A split screen shows two growth curves moving in opposite directions. On the left, the Montgomery boycott starts as a tight knot of friends and widens into a crowd. On the right, Saddleback Church starts as a wide crowd attracted by community and then funnels newcomers into small circles in living rooms. Cards describing Warren's tactics float between the curves for the player to classify.
assets.player_mission: Sort each of Saddleback's tactics by which part of the movement formula it uses: attracting strangers through community appeal, converting them through small-group strong ties, or making them self-directing through new habits. Then decide which mechanism turns casual attendees into self-feeding members.
key_concepts: Rick Warren spent twelve weeks going door-to-door asking strangers why they did not attend church.
Warren fixed practical complaints: music, boring sermons, child care, dress codes, and uncomfortable pews.
Warren replicated the structure of the Montgomery boycott in reverse: attract through weak ties first, then build strong ties.
Warren assigned every Saddleback member to a small group that met weekly in members' homes.
Warren said the weekend crowds are 'just the tip of the iceberg' compared with what happens in small groups during the week.
Saddleback grew to more than twenty thousand weekly parishioners and five thousand small groups.
Small groups alone became little more than a coffee circle without leadership and structure.
Saddleback curriculums teach that 'all of us are simply a bundle of habits' and aim to build Christ-like habits.
Members sign a maturity covenant card promising daily quiet time, tithing 10 percent of income, and small-group membership.
Warren said that once members have new habits, the responsibility for spiritual growth shifts to them because the habits become a new self-identity.
assets.theory_summary: This matrix tests how a self-propelling organization is built by giving members new habits, not by relying on the leader's charisma. Duhigg argues Saddleback grew by running the movement formula in reverse, attracting strangers through weak ties and then making faith self-sustaining by installing habits that reshape identity and ownership.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits)

assets.question: Once a newcomer is attracted to Saddleback by community and weak ties, which mechanism turns that casual attendee into a self-feeding member who no longer needs constant guidance?
assets.column_b_label: New habits that build self-identity and ownership

rows.label: Warren spent twelve weeks fixing complaints about music, sermons, dress codes, and child care to draw the unchurched in.
Every member is assigned to a small group of neighbors that meets weekly in someone's living room.
Members sign a maturity covenant card promising daily quiet time, 10 percent tithing, and small-group membership.
Curriculums teach that people are 'a bundle of habits' and train members in Christ-like habits so they guide themselves.
Warren says the weekend crowd is 'just the tip of the iceberg' compared with what happens inside the small groups.
People attend Saddleback because everyone in their neighborhood and social scene already goes.

distractors: Column a, because comfortable pews alone are what keep a congregation coming back each week.
Column c, because making a few close friends is the same thing as acquiring self-identity.
Column a, because door-to-door recruitment guarantees that newcomers stay forever.
assets.explanation: The focal case sorts to column b: the maturity covenant card and habit-training curriculums install concrete new habits, so members take responsibility for their own spiritual growth and the church no longer has to guide them. Column a describes how newcomers are first attracted, and column c describes the strong-tie small groups that support the habits, but it is the new habits themselves that create a self-directing identity.

assets.topic: Strong-tie ignition of the Montgomery boycott
assets.visual_frame_description: A 1955 Montgomery jailhouse cell at night: Rosa Parks sits in rimless glasses and a brown jacket behind bars. Across the street, a kitchen lit by a bare bulb shows her mother dialing through a mental Rolodex of her daughter's friends. A wall clock ticks from Thursday to Friday as names like Nixon and Durr light up on a map of the city.
assets.player_mission: Diagnose why Parks's arrest could spark a movement when identical arrests had failed, then direct the chain of reactions that turns one jail cell into a Monday boycott. Answer the stage questions and steer the intervention to a successful outcome.
key_concepts: Rosa Parks was arrested on Thursday, December 1, 1955, after refusing to give up her seat on a Montgomery bus driven by James F. Blake.
Geneva Johnson, Viola White, Katie Wingfield, Claudette Colvin, and Mary Louise Smith were arrested for similar seating violations and none sparked a boycott.
Parks was the secretary of the local NAACP chapter and belonged to dozens of social networks across Montgomery.
Parks's friendships spanned the city's hierarchies, from field hands to college professors.
E. D. Nixon, former head of the Montgomery NAACP, and white lawyer Clifford Durr bailed Parks out of jail.
Parks's mother called around to friends, and Nixon's wife phoned her husband, who called Durr, who knew Parks because she had hemmed his daughters' dresses.
There is a natural instinct in friendship that makes people willing to fight for someone they like when they are treated unjustly.
Studies show people have no problem ignoring strangers' injuries, but outrage over a friend's insult can overcome the inertia that makes protests hard to organize.
Jo Ann Robinson called an impromptu meeting close to midnight and suggested a Monday boycott of the city's buses.
Parks's many memberships allowed her friends to muster a response before the community's normal apathy could take hold.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the first part of the movement formula: movements ignite through the social habits of friendship and strong ties. Duhigg argues that Parks's deep community embeddedness let her many friends react before Montgomery's normal apathy could smother the protest, which is why her arrest and not Colvin's or Smith's became a movement.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The central concept is strong-tie ignition: a movement starts when a respected, well-connected person is wronged, because the social habits of friendship instantly mobilize dozens of networks that otherwise stay passive.
assets.stage_1_observation: It is Friday, December 2, 1955. Rosa Parks sits in a Montgomery jail cell, arrested the previous evening on the Cleveland Avenue bus. Across the city her mother is calling through a mental Rolodex of her daughter's friends. On the wall of the precinct hang the arrest records of Geneva Johnson, Viola White, Katie Wingfield, Claudette Colvin, and Mary Louise Smith, each jailed for the same law, none of them followed by a single protest.
assets.stage_1_question: What distinguished Parks from Colvin and Smith so that her arrest alone could trigger a protest?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Parks was deeply embedded in dozens of social networks across Montgomery, from the NAACP and churches to volunteer groups and dressmaking clients, so her many friends could rally a response before the community's normal apathy could take hold.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Hours later, E. D. Nixon and Clifford Durr post bail and ask Parks to let them fight her case in court. Jo Ann Robinson mimeographs flyers and hands them to schoolteachers to distribute to parents and coworkers. You must decide how the chain of friendships and organizations converts one arrest into a Monday boycott that reaches the whole community.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: The friendship habits do the work: teachers pass flyers to parents, ministers announce the protest from every pulpit, and word spreads through the city's hundreds of social organizations so that by Monday the weak ties of the community compel everyone to stay off the buses.

assets.domain: Habit Loops | Behavioral Friction & Choice Architecture
assets.topic: Weak-tie diffusion and peer pressure in communities
assets.visual_frame_description: A late-1960s Harvard sociology lab holds a giant network diagram: dense knots of friends connected by long thin lines to other clusters. Beside it, a printed survey from Granovetter's study of 282 men tallies how each job hunter learned of his opening. A second panel shows a city map where a protest organizer's flyers pool inside one neighborhood and fail to cross the thin lines into the rest of town.
assets.player_mission: Analyze Granovetter's job-hunting data to identify which kind of connection carries the most information, then apply that insight to design a diffusion strategy for a strike. Answer the diagnosis and then choose the intervention that spreads the movement.
key_concepts: Mark Granovetter's late-1960s study tracked how 282 men had found their current employment.
Granovetter called casual acquaintances 'weak ties' because they link people with acquaintances in common who are not directly connected by friendship.
Weak ties give access to social networks where a person does not otherwise belong.
Close friends tend to hear about the same opportunities a person already knows about.
Granovetter wrote that individuals with few weak ties will be deprived of information from distant parts of the social system.
Granovetter argued that without weak ties, momentum generated in a clique does not spread beyond the clique.
Peer pressure spreads through weak ties and gains its authority through communal expectations.
Ignoring the social obligations of a neighborhood endangers access to the social benefits of belonging to a community.
On a playground peer pressure is dangerous, but in adult life it is how business gets done and communities self-organize.
When the strong ties of friendship and the weak ties of peer pressure merge, they create incredible momentum.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the power of weak ties: casual acquaintances connect communities to information and expectations they would never reach through close friends alone. Duhigg argues that movements grow through weak ties because peer pressure travels along those thin connections and gains authority from communal expectations.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The central concept is weak-tie diffusion: information, job leads, opinions, and social pressure spread through casual acquaintances who bridge separate clusters, and a movement that relies only on close friends never breaks out of its clique.
assets.stage_1_observation: You are a graduate student in 1969 reading Mark Granovetter's survey of 282 men who recently changed jobs. His tables show that appeals to strangers were rejected, that close friends helped, and that help came surprisingly often from casual acquaintances. The network diagram makes clear that the men who heard about openings usually got the news from someone they saw only occasionally.
assets.stage_1_question: Why were casual acquaintances, the weak ties, so often the source of a successful job lead?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Because weak ties reach social networks the job hunter does not otherwise belong to, while close friends tend to share the same limited information the job hunter already has.
assets.stage_2_intervention: You are now advising a union trying to spread a strike to workers who have never met the organizers. The organizers are convinced the fastest route is to work only through their own closest friends on the shop floor. Based on the weak-ties finding, what should you tell them to change?
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Recruit through weak-tie networks, such as churches, neighborhood clubs, schools, and other workplaces, so that information and peer pressure flow across the whole community; without weak ties, momentum stays trapped inside the clique and most of the population never hears the call.

assets.domain: Habit Loops | Behavioral Friction & Choice Architecture
assets.topic: Social networks over motives in Freedom Summer
assets.visual_frame_description: A 1980s Arizona archive desk is covered with 720 yellowed Freedom Summer applications. A sociologist runs his finger down columns: motivation answers, marital status, job status, and then a fan of club memberships and contact lists. A map of Mississippi glows on the wall, with three volunteer graves marked outside Longdale.
assets.player_mission: Reconstruct Doug McAdam's analysis of who actually went to Mississippi in 1964. Refute the failed hypotheses, then use the application network data to predict whether a hesitant student boards the bus.
key_concepts: The Mississippi Summer Project, known as Freedom Summer, was a ten-week program in 1964 devoted to registering black voters in the South.
More than a thousand applicants were accepted into Freedom Summer, but more than three hundred of those invited decided to stay home.
White vigilantes killed three volunteers outside Longdale, Mississippi, just a week after the program began.
McAdam read 720 five-page applications that asked about backgrounds, motivations, memberships, and ten people to contact in case of arrest.
McAdam's hypothesis that self-interested students would stay home and other-oriented students would go was wrong.
The selfish and the selfless went South in equal numbers.
Being married or holding a full-time job actually enhanced the applicant's chances of going south.
Participants were enmeshed in communities where both close friends and casual acquaintances expected them to get on the bus.
Among applicants with a religious orientation who belonged to a religious organization, every single one made the trip.
Withdrawing from Freedom Summer once your community knew you were accepted threatened a huge amount of social standing.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests McAdam's conclusion that social networks, not motives or practical costs, determined who participated in Freedom Summer. Duhigg presents the finding as evidence that social habits and the expectations of strong and weak ties, rather than individual conviction, drive participation in dangerous collective action.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The central concept is that participation is predicted by embedding: people go where their friends and acquaintances expect them to go. Motivations and opportunity costs are poor predictors, but the structure of a person's social network predicts action.
assets.stage_1_observation: It is 1985 and Doug McAdam is reading Freedom Summer applications from 1964, when students from Harvard, Yale, and other northern universities volunteered to register black voters in the South. He sorts them into 'self-interested' motives, such as testing oneself or being where the action is, and 'other-oriented' motives, such as improving the lot of blacks or demonstrating the power of nonviolence.
assets.stage_1_question: What did the data show about whether motives or practical obligations could explain who went to Mississippi?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Both explanations failed: the self-interested and the other-oriented went in equal numbers, and being married or holding a full-time job actually increased the chance of going south.
assets.stage_2_intervention: McAdam now maps each applicant's club memberships and the ten people they asked to be kept informed. One applicant, a student with strong religious convictions who belongs to a religious organization, is having second thoughts as departure day nears and her parents urge her to stay home. Predict whether she boards the bus, and why.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: She boards the bus: because she is enmeshed in a religious community whose members all know she was accepted and expect her to go, withdrawing would cost her a huge amount of social standing. McAdam found that every applicant with a religious orientation who belonged to a religious organization made the trip to Mississippi.

assets.domain: Habit Loops | Behavioral Friction & Choice Architecture
assets.visual_frame_description: A 1980 Orange County school auditorium hosts a Sunday service of two hundred people, while in the corner a young pastor clutches the podium, light-headed. A stack of church membership cards sits on a folding table, and a map of the Saddleback Valley shows circles spreading from a small rented condo outward across the fastest-growing region in America.
assets.player_mission: Solve Rick Warren's leadership bottleneck by restructuring the church so it runs without him. First diagnose why the small-group experiment worked, then design the habit system that makes members self-feeders.
key_concepts: Rick Warren planted Saddleback Church in Saddleback Valley, the fastest-growing region in the fastest-growing county in one of the fastest-growing states in America.
Warren started with a prayer group of seven people in his living room.
Warren worked eighteen hours a day, seven days a week, until he collapsed during the 11 A.M. service one December Sunday.
Warren expanded a small experiment in which church members hosted Bible-study classes in their homes.
Warren assigned every Saddleback member to a small group that met every week, transforming participation from a decision into a habit.
Warren said the weekend crowds are 'just the tip of the iceberg' and that 95 percent of the church happens during the week inside small groups.
Without leadership, the small groups were little more than a coffee circle that gossiped about kids.
Saddleback's curriculums were explicitly designed to teach parishioners new habits of faith.
Every Saddleback member signs a maturity covenant card promising daily quiet time, tithing 10 percent of income, and membership in a small group.
Warren's insight was that habits become a new self-identity, at which point members guide themselves and the leader can step back.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests how leaders make an organization self-propelling by installing new habits that create ownership. Duhigg argues that Saddleback scaled because Warren gave every member concrete habits, so spiritual growth no longer depended on his personal attention and members became self-feeders.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The central concept is habit-based delegation: a movement or organization becomes self-sustaining when leaders hand followers new routines and a sense of identity, so the followers no longer need constant guidance and instead take ownership of the enterprise.
assets.stage_1_observation: It is 1980 in Orange County. Rick Warren's rented school-auditorium services have grown past two hundred members in under a year, but Warren works eighteen hours a day answering calls, leading classes, and offering marriage counseling. One Sunday in mid-December he collapses at the podium. He drives to Arizona, recovers from a dark depression, and returns determined to make running the church less work.
assets.stage_1_question: What structural decision allowed Warren to stop being the sole organizer and the bottleneck for the church's growth?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: He assigned every Saddleback member to a small group that met weekly in members' homes, so participation became a habit drawing on existing social urges and the church no longer depended on his personal attention.
assets.stage_2_intervention: The small groups are bonding, but when Warren asks what members discuss, he finds they pray for ten minutes and then spend the rest of the evening talking about kids or gossiping. His goal was to build a community of the faithful, not a coffee circle, and he cannot lead five thousand groups in person. What does he add to make faith itself habitual?
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: He creates habit-training curriculums and a maturity covenant card, promising daily quiet time, tithing 10 percent of income, and small-group membership, so that every member acquires new habits and the responsibility for spiritual growth shifts from Warren to the members themselves.

assets.domain: Habit Loops | Behavioral Friction & Choice Architecture
assets.topic: New habits and self-identity in King's movement
assets.visual_frame_description: A Montgomery night in early 1956: King's house on South Jackson Street has a shattered front window and a crater in the porch. A crowd of several hundred black residents presses forward under the glare of police lights, a bottle arcs through the air, and a policeman raises a baton. King steps onto the porch, arms open, as the crowd hushes.
assets.player_mission: Keep the yearlong boycott from collapsing by understanding how King's new habits made the movement self-propelling. First diagnose why the protest's early resolve was failing, then choose the intervention that converts followers into self-directing leaders.
key_concepts: Within a few weeks of the boycott, King worried openly that the ability of the Negro community to continue the struggle was in doubt.
The police commissioner threatened taxi drivers, and drivers began dropping out of the boycott's carpool.
The boycott's leaders signed up two hundred volunteers to participate in a carpool.
A bomb exploded at King's house while his wife, Coretta, and infant daughter were inside.
King told the crowd 'don't get your weapons' and that he who lives by the sword shall perish by the sword.
King gave the movement a new lens: this was not a war but an embrace, and participants could show allegiance by adopting new habits.
King cast the boycott as part of God's plan, the same destiny that ended British colonialism in India and slavery in the United States.
The week after the bombing, two dozen new drivers signed up for the carpool and people began self-organizing and taking leadership.
When ninety people were indicted, almost all of them rushed to the courthouse to present themselves for arrest.
Branch described the mass meetings as similar to Alcoholics Anonymous, where people learn new habits by watching others demonstrate them.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the third part of the movement formula: a movement endures when leaders give participants new habits that create a fresh identity and a feeling of ownership. Duhigg argues that King's recasting of the struggle converted followers into self-directing leaders, making the boycott a self-propelling force that outlived his personal guidance.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The central concept is identity-shaping habits: when a leader gives people new routines and a new way to see themselves, they stop acting because they were told to and start acting because the cause has become who they are.
assets.stage_1_observation: It is early 1956 and the Montgomery boycott is weeks old. The police commissioner has threatened to arrest taxi drivers who carry black passengers at a discount, so the leaders set up a carpool, and the police respond by issuing tickets and harassing people at meeting spots. Drivers begin dropping out. From early morning to late night King's telephone rings, and he confesses doubt about the community's ability to continue the struggle.
assets.stage_1_question: What did King do to keep the protest from collapsing as resolve began to wane?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: He recast the boycott as part of God's plan and a movement of love rather than war, handing people new habits and a new lens, so participants took ownership of the struggle and began to lead themselves.
assets.stage_2_intervention: A bomb explodes at King's house with his wife and infant daughter inside. A crowd of several hundred gathers as police shout for them to disperse. Someone shoves a cop, a bottle flies through the air, and a policeman swings a baton. The police chief, who publicly supported the White Citizens' Council, asks King to stop a riot from breaking out. What does King do?
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: He steps onto the porch and preaches nonviolence, telling the crowd not to get their weapons and to love their white brothers, and the crowd quietly walks home. The next week two dozen new drivers join the carpool and the movement becomes self-organizing, fueled by people who act because they have taken ownership of the cause.

assets.topic: The weak-tie job referral and communal obligations
assets.visual_frame_description: A modern office kitchenette at Meridian Analytics. Maya, a midlevel product manager in a gray blazer, stands with her phone pressed to her ear while a coworker sips coffee in the background. On her screen, a calendar shows a job interview slot opening up on her boss Dana's calendar for a new data lead.
assets.player_mission: Take the call from Liam, an acquaintance from another company who shares friends with you but is not a close friend. Decide how much of your reputation and energy to spend helping a friend of a friend land a job, and respond in the way the social habits of communities reward.
key_concepts: In Granovetter's study, job hunters often received help from casual acquaintances who were neither strangers nor close pals.
Weak ties give access to social networks where a person does not otherwise belong.
Close friends tend to know the same job openings a person already knows about.
Peer pressure spreads through weak ties and gains its authority through communal expectations.
If you ignore the social obligations of your network, you endanger access to the social benefits that come from belonging to a community.
If you refuse to help, word can travel through acquaintances and damage your reputation as a team player.
On a playground peer pressure is dangerous, but in adult life it is how business gets done and communities self-organize.
A sense of obligation compels people to act even when they do not necessarily want to participate.
When the strong ties of friendship and the weak ties of peer pressure merge, they create incredible momentum.
Communities reward those who honor their social obligations and penalize those who shrug off expected patterns.
assets.theory_summary: This dialogue simulates the power of weak ties and communal obligation in professional life: casual acquaintances bridge networks, and helping them honors the social habits that keep communities self-organizing. Duhigg argues that such obligations gain authority through communal expectations, and ignoring them risks your standing in exactly the circles where business gets done.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits)

assets.scenario_setup: You are Maya, a midlevel product manager at Meridian Analytics, a growing software firm. Your boss Dana is hiring a data lead, and you have a strong reputation as a team player. It is Wednesday afternoon when your phone buzzes with an unfamiliar number. The caller is Liam Chen, a data engineer at another company. You met him once at a mutual friend's wedding through your former classmate Priya, and you share a few friends in common but do not know each other well. Liam is asking you to put in a good word with Dana about the open position.
dialogue: Liam (on the phone): 'Hi Maya, this is Liam Chen. We met at the Henderson wedding, through Priya. I'm sorry to call out of the blue, but I heard Meridian is hiring a data lead.'
Maya (you): 'Oh, right, Liam — Priya's friend from her old team. Good to hear from you. What can I do for you?'
Liam: 'I'd love to be considered for that data lead role. I know we don't know each other well, but I was hoping you might be willing to put in a good word with your boss.'
Maya (you): 'That's a big ask from someone I've only met once, Liam.'
Liam: 'I get that. I just thought, since we run in the same circles through Priya, you might be able to tell me honestly whether it's worth applying.'
Maya (you): 'Well, tell me a bit about your background first.'
Liam: 'Eight years in data engineering, led the migration at Northgate last year. I'm happy to send you my resume before you say anything to anyone.'
choices: I'll be honest, Liam: I barely know you, so I can't risk my reputation vouching for a stranger. Good luck with the application.
Send me your resume. If it's genuine, I'll mention your name to Dana as someone Priya and I know well. Happy to help a friend of a friend.
I'll forward your resume to Dana with no comment at all, so I'm not really sticking my neck out for you.
If Priya asked you to call me, then she should be the one making the introduction, not me.
assets.theoretical_principle: The power of weak ties combined with the social habits of communal obligation: casual acquaintances bridge networks you do not belong to, and communities expect you to honor the obligations of mutual acquaintance.
assets.psychological_breakdown: Choice 1 is optimal because it honors the weak-tie relationship at low cost: you verify substance first, then extend access to your network, exactly the behavior Granovetter found carries job leads across communities. Refusing outright (choice 0) treats a weak tie as a stranger and risks the tennis-partner effect where word of your refusal travels and damages your reputation as a team player. Forwarding without endorsement (choice 2) half-participates and still burns the social bridge, while choice 3 deflects the obligation onto Priya and signals that you shrug off the expected patterns of your community.

assets.visual_frame_description: A bright Austin co-working space in the evening. Priya, the founder of a civic start-up called BlockBright, sits across from Devon, a well-connected resident in his forties who volunteers at his kids' school, the PTA, and his church. A whiteboard behind them shows a map of neighborhoods with faded checkmarks, and a stack of unassigned captain badges sits on the table.
assets.player_mission: Run the conversation with Devon, a resident you only know casually, to turn BlockBright's monthly volunteer days into a self-sustaining movement. Choose the response that gives Devon concrete new habits and ownership instead of relying on guilt, coercion, or your own constant effort.
key_concepts: A movement endures when leaders give participants new habits that create a fresh sense of identity and a feeling of ownership.
Usually only when all three parts of the movement process are fulfilled can a movement become self-propelling and reach critical mass.
For an idea to grow beyond a community, it must become self-propelling, and the surest way is to give people new habits that help them figure out where to go on their own.
Small groups and assigned roles transform participation from a decision into a habit.
Warren's curriculums and maturity covenant card made members self-feeders by making habits a new self-identity.
McAdam found that motives did not predict participation; embedding in communities with expectations did.
Weak ties spread information and peer pressure across neighborhoods that close friends cannot reach.
People are more likely to act when their community expects them to, because ignoring social obligations risks social standing.
Rick Warren's insight was that a leader can step back once followers guide themselves through habit.
King grew the boycott by handing protesters new habits and a new identity, making the movement self-perpetuating.
assets.theory_summary: This dialogue tests how leaders make a movement self-propelling by installing new habits and ownership, the third part of Duhigg's movement formula. Relying on moral appeals or your own constant effort keeps you as the bottleneck, while giving a participant a concrete recurring routine and a titled identity converts a follower into a self-directing leader.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits)

assets.scenario_setup: Priya runs BlockBright, a start-up that organizes monthly neighborhood cleanups in Austin. The cleanups only happen when she personally chases volunteers, and she is burning out. She has a core group of six close friends who always show up, but the movement cannot scale. Her idea is to create 'captains' who own the second Sunday of each month in their block. She only knows Devon casually, through the PTA and mutual neighbors, but he is exactly the kind of well-connected person who could carry the program. She has asked him to coffee to recruit him as a captain.
dialogue: Priya: 'Devon, thanks for meeting me. The captains are the heart of where I want to take BlockBright — I just can't keep recruiting every single month by hand.'
Devon: 'I get it, and I like what you guys do. But I've got two kids and a job. What exactly would I be signing up for?'
Priya: 'That's fair. Let me be honest about what I need from you, and what you'd get out of it.'
Devon: 'Okay, I'm listening. My Sundays are precious, so whatever I commit to has to be predictable.'
Priya: 'Predictable is exactly the point. I want you to own your block, not just volunteer at it.'
Devon: 'What does owning the block actually mean on a Tuesday, though?'
choices: Just agree to coordinate the second Sunday on your block — I'll send you the list of names and everyone else already said yes.

Here's the plan: one twenty-minute check-in each Sunday, a printed captain card with your three tasks, and I'll ask your PTA and church friends to help you build the roster. You own it, and I step back.
You can come on the days you can and text me when you can't — I'll handle the rest, so there's no real pressure on you.
Think of it as paying it forward for the whole city, Devon. Honestly, that's really all the reason you need.
assets.theoretical_principle: The third part of the movement formula: leaders give participants new habits that create identity and ownership, making the movement self-propelling rather than dependent on the leader.
assets.psychological_breakdown: Choice 1 is optimal because it installs a concrete recurring habit (the weekly check-in), gives Devon a titled identity and tools (the captain card), and recruits through his weak ties (PTA and church), so BlockBright stops depending on Priya. Choice 0 leans on coercion and an unearned 'everyone said yes' claim, which cannot sustain ownership. Choice 2 keeps Priya as the organizer and hands Devon an exit, preserving the bottleneck. Choice 3 relies on a moral motive, and McAdam's data showed motives alone never predicted who actually showed up.
